claim: HIV-1 accesses the nuclear DNA of interphase cells via a poorly defined process involving functional interactions between the capsid protein (CA) and nucleoporins (Nups).
source: HIV-1 accesses the nuclear DNA of interphase cells via a poorly defined process involving functional interactions between the capsid protein (CA) and nucleoporins (Nups).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact about HIV-1 infection mechanism.

claim: HIV-1 CA can bind multiple Nups.
source: Here, we show that HIV-1 CA can bind multiple Nups
evidence: The authors present data showing CA binding to multiple Nups in their experiments.

claim: Both natural and manipulated variation in Nup levels impacts HIV-1 infection in a manner that is dependent on cell-type, cell-cycle, and cyclophilin A (CypA).
source: both natural and manipulated variation in Nup levels impacts HIV-1 infection in a manner that is strikingly dependent on cell-type, cell-cycle, and cyclophilin A (CypA).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing these dependencies.

claim: Nups mediate the function of the antiviral protein MX2.
source: We also show that Nups mediate the function of the antiviral protein MX2
evidence: The authors demonstrate through experiments that Nups are required for MX2 function.

claim: MX2 can variably inhibit non-viral NLS function.
source: MX2 can variably inhibit non-viral NLS function
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing MX2 inhibits nuclear import driven by certain NLS sequences.

claim: Both enhancing and inhibiting effects of cyclophilin A and MX2 on various HIV-1 CA mutants could be induced or abolished by manipulating levels of the Nup93 subcomplex, the Nup62 subcomplex, NUP88, NUP214, RANBP2, or NUP153.
source: Remarkably, both enhancing and inhibiting effects of cyclophilin A and MX2 on various HIV-1 CA mutants could be induced or abolished by manipulating levels of the Nup93 subcomplex, the Nup62 subcomplex, NUP88, NUP214, RANBP2, or NUP153.
evidence: The authors present experimental data showing these effects through siRNA knockdown experiments.

claim: Several Nup-dependent 'pathways' are variably exploited by HIV-1 to target host DNA in a cell-type, cell-cycle, CypA and CA-sequence dependent manner.
source: Our findings suggest that several Nup-dependent 'pathways' are variably exploited by HIV-1 to target host DNA in a cell-type, cell-cycle, CypA and CA-sequence dependent manner
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their experimental findings.

claim: Nup-dependent pathways are differentially inhibited by MX2.
source: and are differentially inhibited by MX2.
evidence: The authors infer this from their experimental data showing variable MX2 effects.

claim: The viral capsid (CA) is the key viral determinant of the ability of HIV-1 to infect non-dividing cells.
source: The viral capsid (CA) is the key viral determinant of the ability of HIV-1 to infect non-dividing cells (Yamashita and Emerman, 2004)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: CA mutants can specifically disrupt the ability of HIV-1 to infect non-dividing cells.
source: CA mutants can specifically disrupt the ability of HIV-1 to infect non-dividing cells (Yamashita et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Cyclophilin A (CypA) is a cellular CA-interacting protein that has been suggested to regulate or otherwise influence HIV-1 nuclear import and infection.
source: In addition to CA itself, cellular CA-interacting proteins have been suggested to regulate or otherwise influence HIV-1 nuclear import and infection, including the peptidylprolyl isomerase cyclophilin A (CypA)
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge in the introduction.

claim: CPSF6 is a cellular CA-interacting protein that has been suggested to regulate or otherwise influence HIV-1 nuclear import and infection.
source: cellular CA-interacting proteins have been suggested to regulate or otherwise influence HIV-1 nuclear import and infection, including...the mRNA processing protein cleavage and polyadenylation specificity factor 6 (CPSF6) (De Iaco et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2010; Price et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: CA can directly interact with NUP153 and RANBP2.
source: CA can also directly interact with two nucleoporins (Nups) NUP153 and RANBP2(NUP358), that appear to play a major role in HIV-1 nuclear import (Bichel et al., 2013; Di Nunzio et al., 2013; Lin et al., 2013; Matreyek et al., 2013; Schaller et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: NUP153 and RANBP2 appear to play a major role in HIV-1 nuclear import.
source: CA can also directly interact with two nucleoporins (Nups) NUP153 and RANBP2(NUP358), that appear to play a major role in HIV-1 nuclear import (Bichel et al., 2013; Di Nunzio et al., 2013; Lin et al., 2013; Matreyek et al., 2013; Schaller et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: A number of other Nups or nuclear transport receptors have been implicated as co-factors for HIV-1 infection in genome-wide RNA interference screens.
source: A number of other Nups or nuclear transport receptors have also been implicated as co-factors for HIV-1 infection in genome-wide RNA interference screens (Brass et al., 2008; König et al., 2008; Yeung et al., 2009; Zhou et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous genome-wide screens.

claim: CA-dependent interactions with Nups appear to play a role in determining where HIV-1 proviral DNA is integrated into the host genome.
source: CA-dependent interactions with Nups also appear to play a role in determining where HIV-1 proviral DNA is integrated into the host genome (Di Nunzio et al., 2013; Koh et al., 2013; Ocwieja et al., 2011; Schaller et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Approximately 30 distinct Nups are present in the nuclear pore complex (NPC).
source: Approximately, 30 distinct Nups are present in the nuclear pore complex (NPC) that is organized in repetitively arranged subcomplexes with 8-fold rotational symmetry.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about NPC structure.

claim: The NPC is organized in repetitively arranged subcomplexes with 8-fold rotational symmetry.
source: Approximately, 30 distinct Nups are present in the nuclear pore complex (NPC) that is organized in repetitively arranged subcomplexes with 8-fold rotational symmetry.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about NPC structure.

claim: The NPC has a tripartite architecture, with a central major architectural scaffold, cytoplasmic filaments, and the nuclear basket.
source: The NPC has a tripartite architecture, with a central major architectural scaffold, that includes the transmembrane Nups, the Nup107, Nup93, and Nup62 subcomplexes. The NPC is appended with cytoplasmic filaments, and the nuclear basket (an assembly of 8 intranuclear filaments joined into a basket) (Fernandez-Martinez and Rout, 2012; Hoelz et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations describing NPC structure.

claim: Some NPC components are dynamic, with scaffold Nups remaining associated for hours to days while FG repeat Nups are associated only for minutes at a time.
source: Although NPCs are generally depicted as static structures, some components are dynamic. Specifically, the scaffold Nups remain associated with the NPC for hours to days while other components, including the phenylalanine-glycine (FG) repeat Nups, are associated with the NPC only for minutes at a time (Morchoisne-Bolhy et al., 2015; Rabut et al., 2004a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on NPC dynamics.

claim: Recent structural studies suggest the existence of conformational flexibility in the main architectural elements of the NPC.
source: Recent structural studies suggest the existence of conformational flexibility in the main architectural elements of the NPC (the Nup107 or Y complex, the Nup62 complex, and the Nup93 complex or linker Nups) (reviewed in (Knockenhauer and Schwartz, 2016)).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: A number of reports have pointed to compositional variability of the NPC both within and between cells.
source: Moreover, a number of reports have also pointed to compositional variability of the NPC both within and between cells (D'Angelo et al., 2009; Gomez-Cavazos and Hetzer, 2015; Lowe et al., 2015; Lupu et al., 2008; Ori et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Nup expression can be altered under certain conditions, such as upon IFN stimulation.
source: and altered expression under certain conditions, such as upon IFN stimulation (Enninga et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: NPCs with different compositions may be poised for the transport of different cargos.
source: These reports raise the intriguing possibility that NPCs with different compositions may be poised for the transport of different cargos.
evidence: This is a speculation based on previous reports of NPC heterogeneity.

claim: MX2 localizes to the NPC.
source: MX2, an antiviral protein whose expression is strongly upregulated by type 1 interferon, localizes to the NPC (Goujon et al., 2013; Kane et al., 2013; King et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: MX2 expression is strongly upregulated by type 1 interferon.
source: MX2, an antiviral protein whose expression is strongly upregulated by type 1 interferon
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about MX2.

claim: MX2 is comprised of a GTPase domain connected to a carboxy-terminal stalk domain via a tripartite bundle-signaling element (BSE).
source: Like the better-studied MX1 protein, MX2 is comprised of a GTPase domain connected to a carboxy-terminal stalk domain via a tripartite bundle-signaling element (BSE) (Haller et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation describing MX2 structure.

claim: MX2 contains an NLS-like sequence in its first 25 amino acids that is required for NPC localization.
source: Unlike MX1, MX2 contains an NLS-like sequence in its first 25 amino acids that is required for NPC localization (Kane et al., 2013; King et al., 2004; Melén et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: MX2 was recently shown to inhibit infection by HIV-1 and other primate lentiviruses.
source: MX1 can inhibit a number of viruses, but not retroviruses (Haller et al., 2015), while MX2 was recently shown to inhibit infection by HIV-1 and other primate lentiviruses. (Goujon et al., 2013; Kane et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The antiretroviral activity and specificity of MX2 is governed by the N-terminal domain that is absent in MX1.
source: The antiretroviral activity and specificity of MX2 is governed by the N-terminal domain that is absent in MX1 (Busnadiego et al., 2014; Goujon et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: GTPase function and higher order oligomerization are generally required for the antiviral activity of MX1 but are dispensable for the antiviral activity of MX2.
source: Moreover, GTPase function and higher order oligomerization are generally required for the antiviral activity of MX1 (Haller et al., 2015) but are dispensable for the antiviral activity of MX2 (Dicks et al., 2016; Fribourgh et al., 2014; Goujon et al., 2014, 2013; Kane et al., 2013; Matreyek et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: MX2 inhibits HIV-1 infection after the completion of reverse transcription but prior to the chromosomal integration of viral DNA.
source: MX2 inhibits HIV-1 infection after the completion of reverse transcription but prior to the chromosomal integration of viral DNA (Goujon et al., 2013; Kane et al., 2013; Matreyek et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: MX2 inhibits HIV-1 infection more potently in non-dividing cells.
source: and because MX2 inhibits HIV-1 infection more potently in non-dividing cells (Kane et al., 2013; Yamashita and Emerman, 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Current models suggest that MX2 acts by preventing nuclear import of the viral preintegration complex.
source: For this reason, and because MX2 inhibits HIV-1 infection more potently in non-dividing cells (Kane et al., 2013; Yamashita and Emerman, 2009), current models suggest that MX2 acts by preventing nuclear import of the viral preintegration complex.
evidence: This is stated as the current understanding in the field, supported by citations.

claim: The viral capsid is the major viral determinant of MX2 sensitivity.
source: Additionally, the viral capsid is the major viral determinant of MX2 sensitivity
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Several single amino-acid substitutions in CA have been identified that confer partial or complete resistance to MX2.
source: and several single amino-acid substitutions in CA have been identified that confer partial or complete resistance to MX2 (Busnadiego et al., 2014; Goujon et al., 2013; Kane et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2013, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: MX2 has been found to directly bind the HIV-1 CA.
source: MX2 has also been found to directly bind the HIV-1 CA, but the relevance of this binding for viral inhibition is unclear, as MX2-resistant CA proteins are also bound by MX2 (Fribourgh et al., 2014; Fricke et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: MX2-resistant CA proteins are also bound by MX2.
source: MX2 has also been found to directly bind the HIV-1 CA, but the relevance of this binding for viral inhibition is unclear, as MX2-resistant CA proteins are also bound by MX2 (Fribourgh et al., 2014; Fricke et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Many CA mutations conferring MX2 resistance are also known to affect binding to and/or requirements for CypA, CPSF6, NUP153, and RANBP2.
source: Notably, many of the CA mutations conferring partial or complete MX2 resistance, such as G89V, N57A/S, N74D, and A92E, are also known to affect binding to and/or requirements for cellular proteins implicated in HIV-1 nuclear import including CypA, CPSF6, NUP153, and RANBP2 (Hatziioannou et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2010; Matreyek et al., 2013; Rihn et al., 2013; Schaller et al., 2011; Sokolskaja et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: CA mutants conferring MX2 resistance alter infection in non-dividing cells and/or alter integration site selection.
source: These mutants alter infection in non-dividing cells, and/or altere integration site selection, suggesting the possibility that they may utilize distinct pathways to access nuclear DNA.
evidence: This is stated as an observation that leads to speculation about distinct pathways.

claim: MX2 antiviral activity is affected by CypA.
source: MX2 antiviral activity is also affected by CypA
evidence: This is stated as a known fact.

claim: CypA is a ubiquitous and abundantly expressed member of a family of peptidyl-prolyl isomerases.
source: CypA, a ubiquitous and abundantly expressed member of a family of peptidyl-prolyl isomerases, whose role in HIV-1 infection is enigmatic (Luban et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by a citation.

claim: Disruption of the interaction between HIV-1 and CypA reduces the efficiency of HIV-1 infection.
source: Disruption of the interaction between HIV-1 and CypA, either genetically or by cyclosporine A (CsA) addition, reduces the efficiency of HIV-1 infection (reviewed in (Campbell and Hope, 2015))
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Some studies have indicated that CypA-CA interactions influence nuclear entry.
source: and some studies have indicated that CypA-CA interactions influence nuclear entry (De Iaco and Luban, 2014; Schaller et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: CsA treatment has diverse enhancing and inhibiting effects on infection that are determined by CA mutations and target cell type.
source: However, defining a precise role for CypA in HIV-1 infection has proved difficult because CsA treatment has diverse enhancing and inhibiting effects on infection that are determined by CA mutations and target cell type (reviewed in (Campbell and Hope, 2015; Yamashita and Engelman, 2017)).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: For HIV-1WT, MX2 antiviral potency was enhanced by growth-arrest in HeLa cells.
source: For HIV-1WT, MX2 antiviral potency was enhanced by growth-arrest in HeLa cells, similar to our previous findings in HOS and K562 cells (Kane et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1 and a citation to previous work.

claim: Growth-arrest caused only a marginal increase in MX2 potency in HT1080 cells.
source: However, growth-arrest caused only a marginal increase in MX2 potency in HT1080 cells.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: HIV-1WT was largely unaffected by CsA addition in HeLa cells.
source: As expected from previous work (Hatziioannou et al., 2005; Sokolskaja et al., 2004), HIV-1WT was largely unaffected by CsA addition in HeLa cells
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1 and citations to previous work.

claim: HIV-1WT infectivity was reduced upon CsA addition in both HT1080 and HOS cells.
source: but its infectivity was reduced upon CsA addition in both HT1080 and HOS cells (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: CsA addition abolished the anti-viral activity of MX2 in both HeLa and HT1080 cells.
source: CsA addition abolished the anti-viral activity of MX2 in both HeLa and HT1080 cells, suggesting that MX2 is active only against CypA bound or modified HIV-1WT capsids in these contexts.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1 and the authors' interpretation.

claim: HIV-2 and SIVmac were less sensitive to MX2 in dividing HeLa, HOS, and HT1080 cells than HIV-1.
source: HIV-2 and the simian immunodeficiency virus SIVmac, were less sensitive to MX2 in dividing HeLa, HOS, and HT1080 cells than HIV-1 ((Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and (Kane et al., 2013)).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and a citation.

claim: Arresting cell division in HeLa, and especially in HT1080 cells, reduced rather than enhanced MX2 antiviral potency against HIV-2 and SIVmac.
source: Moreover, and in contrast to effects on HIV-1WT, arresting cell division in HeLa, and especially in HT1080 cells, reduced rather than enhanced MX2 antiviral potency against HIV-2 and SIVmac.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: CsA addition did not affect HIV-2 or SIVmac infection and did not affect MX2 potency against these viruses.
source: As expected, CsA addition (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) did not affect HIV-2 or SIV mac infection and did not affect MX2 potency against these viruses.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The HIV-1G94D and HIV-1A92E CA mutations confer CsA dependence in some cell lines, including HeLa, but confer CsA resistance in others, including HOS and HT1080 cells.
source: The HIV-1G94D and HIV-1A92E CA mutations confer CsA dependence (i.e. their infection is inhibited by CA:CypA binding) during early replication steps in some cell lines, including HeLa, but confer CsA resistance in others, including HOS (Hatziioannou et al., 2005; Sokolskaja et al., 2004) and HT1080 cells (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 3, and citations to previous work.

claim: Both HIV-1G94D and HIV-1A92E exhibited reduced sensitivity to MX2 compared to HIV-1WT in HeLa and HOS cells.
source: Both HIV-1G94D and HIV-1A92E exhibited reduced sensitivity to MX2 compared to HIV-1WT in HeLa (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and HOS cells (Kane et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2, and a citation.

claim: HIV-1WT, HIV-1G94D, and HIV-1A92E exhibited equivalent MX2 sensitivity in HT1080 cells.
source: Conversely, HIV-1WT, HIV-1G94D, and HIV-1A92E exhibited equivalent MX2 sensitivity in HT1080 cells.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: HIV-1G94D and HIV-1A92E mutants retained residual sensitivity to MX2 in the presence of CsA.
source: Moreover, unlike HIV-1WT, the HIV-1G94D and HIV-1A92E mutants retained residual sensitivity to MX2 in the presence of CsA (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The HIV-1T210K CA mutant was selected by passage in MT4 cells expressing MX2 and exhibits resistance to inhibition by MX2 in that context.
source: The HIV-1T210K CA mutant was selected by passage in MT4 cells expressing MX2 and exhibits resistance to inhibition by MX2 in that context (Busnadiego et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: HIV-1T210K was MX2-resistant in HeLa cells but became sensitive to MX2 when HeLa cells were growth arrested.
source: HIV-1T210K was similarly MX2-resistant in HeLa cells but, surprisingly, became sensitive to MX2 when HeLa cells were growth arrested.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: HIV-1T210K was CsA-dependent in HeLa cells, but not in HT1080 or HOS cells.
source: HIV-1T210K was CsA-dependent, in that it was rendered more infectious upon CsA addition in HeLa cells, but not in HT1080 or HOS cells.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: CsA addition conferred increased sensitivity of HIV-1T210K to MX2 in both HeLa and HT1080 cells.
source: However, unlike HIV-1WT, CsA addition conferred increased sensitivity of HIV-1T210K to MX2 in both HeLa and HT1080 cells (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The acquired MX2 resistance of HIV-1T210K is cell-type-, cell-cycle-, and CypA-dependent.
source: Thus, although the HIV-1T210K mutant arose under selective pressure from MX2, the acquired resistance is cell-type-, cell-cycle-, and CypA-dependent.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their data.

claim: The G208R mutant was only partly resistant to MX2 in HeLa or HT1080 cells.
source: Similarly, the G208R mutant, which also arose under selective pressure imposed by MX2 in MT4 cells (Busnadiego et al., 2014) was only partly resistant to MX2 in HeLa or HT1080 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and a citation.

claim: HIV-1N74D, whose CA does not interact with CPSF6, was less sensitive than HIV-1WT to MX2 in HeLa and HT1080 cells.
source: HIV-1N74D, whose CA does not interact with CPSF6 (Lee et al., 2010), was less sensitive than HIV-1WT to MX2 in HeLa and HT1080 cells (as well as in HOS cells (Goujon et al., 2013; Kane et al., 2013)).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1 and citations to previous work.

claim: HIV-1N74D was CsA sensitive in all three cell lines (HeLa, HT1080, HOS), particularly when cells were growth arrested.
source: HIV-1N74D was also CsA sensitive in all three cell lines (Ambrose et al., 2012), particularly when cells were growth arrested.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1 and a citation.

claim: CsA treatment abolished the MX2 sensitivity of HIV-1N74D, and even caused MX2 to modestly increase HIV-1N74D infection, particularly in non-dividing HT1080 cells.
source: However, CsA treatment abolished the MX2 sensitivity of HIV-1N74D, and even caused MX2 to modestly increase HIV-1N74D infection, particularly in non-dividing HT1080 cells (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: Modest enhancement of infection by MX2 was observed for the HIV-1G89V whose capsid does not bind CypA, in both HeLa and HT1080 cells, irrespective of cell-division.
source: Modest enhancement of infection by MX2 was also observed for the HIV-1G89V whose capsid does not bind CypA (Wiegers et al., 1999), in both HeLa and HT1080 cells, and irrespective of cell-division (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1 and a citation.

claim: HIV-1N57S is unable to efficiently infect non-dividing cells and is MX2 resistant.
source: A particularly striking phenotype was observed with the HIV-1N57S CA mutant, which is unable to efficiently infect non-dividing cells (Rihn et al., 2013) and is MX2 resistant.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: HIV-1N57S infection was unaffected by either CsA or MX2 in HeLa cells.
source: While HIV-1N57S infection was unaffected by either CsA or MX2 in HeLa cells
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: HIV-1N57S was exquisitely sensitive to CsA (~20 fold inhibition) in HT1080 cells.
source: HIV-1N57S was exquisitely sensitive to CsA (~20 fold inhibition) in HT1080 cells.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: MX2 completely reversed the dramatic reduction in HIV-1N57S infectivity caused by CsA in HT1080 cells.
source: Remarkably, this dramatic reduction in infectivity was completely reversed by MX2.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: MX2 increased infection by the HIV-1N57S mutant when CypA:CA interaction was inhibited.
source: In other words, MX2 increased infection by the HIV-1N57S mutant when CypA:CA interaction was inhibited (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: MX2 and CypA can either inhibit or enhance HIV-1 infection.
source: These experiments demonstrate that MX2 and CypA can either inhibit or enhance HIV-1 infection.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their experimental data.

claim: The effects of MX2 and CypA varied in a cell-type, cell-cycle and CA-sequence dependent manner.
source: Their effects clearly varied in a cell-type, cell-cycle and CA-sequence dependent manner.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their experimental data.

claim: Both the viral capsid and some feature of the cellular environment determine whether MX2 and CypA inhibit or enhance HIV-1 infection.
source: Thus, both the viral capsid, and some feature of the cellular environment that varies in the aforementioned cell lines, presumably other cellular factor(s), determine whether MX2 and CypA inhibit or enhance HIV-1 infection.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation and speculation based on their data.

claim: Several striking differences in the levels of individual Nups were found among a panel of cell lines.
source: We found several striking differences in the levels of individual Nups among this panel of cell lines (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The monocytic THP-1 and U937 cells expressed lower levels of almost all Nups than other cell lines.
source: For example, the monocytic THP-1 and U937 cells expressed lower levels of almost all Nups than other cell lines, suggesting that they may have fewer nuclear pores.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2 and the authors' interpretation.

claim: HT1080 cells did not express detectable levels of NUP210.
source: Additionally, HT1080 cells did not express detectable levels of NUP210.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Natural target cells of HIV-1 infection, namely primary CD4+ T cells and macrophages, exhibited differences in nucleoporin expression levels.
source: We also found that natural target cells of HIV-1 infection, namely primary CD4+ T cells and macrophages exhibited differences in nucleoporin expression levels (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: Dramatically higher levels of NUP37 were found in primary macrophages as compared to MT4, THP-1, and primary CD4+ T cells.
source: For example, dramatically higher levels of NUP37 were found in primary macrophages as compared to MT4, THP-1, and primary CD4+ T cells
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Lower levels of NUP210 were present in macrophages.
source: while lower levels of NUP210 were present in macrophages.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The appearance of unanticipated anti-Nup antibody reactive species in some cell lines and in primary cells suggested potential differences in the expression of alternative isoforms of several Nups.
source: The appearance of unanticipated anti-Nup antibody reactive species in some cell lines and in primary cells suggested potential differences in the expression of alternative isoforms of several Nups (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their western blot data, with a caveat about non-specific binding.

claim: Marked compositional heterogeneity of NPCs occurs between cell types.
source: These results are consistent with previous studies reporting cell-type dependent differences in Nup expression (D'Angelo et al., 2009; Gomez-Cavazos and Hetzer, 2015; Lowe et al., 2015; Lupu et al., 2008; Ori et al., 2013) and suggest that marked compositional heterogeneity of NPCs occurs between cell types.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their data, supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Variation in Nup levels has the potential to affect HIV-1 infection and its modulation by cell-cycle, CypA, and MX2.
source: In any case, variation in Nup levels has the potential to affect HIV-1 infection and its modulation by cell-cycle, CypA, and MX2.
evidence: This is the authors' speculation based on their observations.

claim: CPSF6 was detected in the CA-tube bound fractions and was entirely depleted from the cellular lysates by WT CA tubes.
source: Notably, CPSF6 was detected in the CA-tube bound fractions (lane 5 Figure 3) and, in fact, was entirely depleted from the cellular lysates by WT CA tubes (compare lanes 2 and 3, Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Almost complete depletion from cell lysates was observed for NUP62, NUP88, and NUP153, suggesting that these proteins are tightly bound to the CA tubes.
source: Similarly, almost complete depletion from cell lysates was observed for NUP62, NUP88, and NUP153, suggesting that these proteins are tightly bound to the CA tubes.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3 and the authors' interpretation.

claim: RANBP2 was bound to CA tubes, but a significant fraction of this protein remained in the unbound supernatant.
source: RANBP2 was also bound to CA tubes, but a significant fraction of this protein remained in the unbound supernatant.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Little or no binding was detected for NUP107, NUP133, and NUP155.
source: Nevertheless, not all Nups interacted with CA tubes, as little or no binding was detected for NUP107, NUP133, and NUP155.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Expression of MX2 confirmed a robust interaction between MX2 and the viral CA tubes.
source: Finally, expression of MX2 following doxycycline addition also confirmed a robust interaction between MX2 and the viral CA tubes (lane 10, Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: MX2 expression did not detectably affect the interaction between Nups and CA tubes.
source: MX2 expression did not detectably affect the interaction between Nups and CA tubes (compare lanes 5 and 10, Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: NUP153 remained localized to the nuclear envelope following knockdown of each of the other Nups.
source: Strikingly, NUP153 remained localized at the nuclear envelope following knockdown of each of the other Nups.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplements 1–6.

claim: NUP153 recruitment to the nuclear envelope is an early event during nuclear pore formation, and its incorporation into the nuclear envelope is not expected to be dependent on other Nups.
source: This finding is likely a reflection of the fact that NUP153 recruitment to the nuclear envelope is an early event during nuclear pore formation, and its incorporation into the nuclear envelope is not therefore expected to be dependent on other Nups (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplements 1–6) (Bodoor et al., 1999; Vollmer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Several Nup siRNA knockdowns caused mislocalization of RANBP2, NUP214, NUP62, and/or NUP98.
source: In contrast, several Nup siRNA knockdowns caused mislocalization of RANBP2, NUP214, NUP62, and/or NUP98 (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplements 1–14).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplements 1–14.

claim: Depletion of Nups known to participate in the early stages of NPC formation or those known to form the structural scaffold of the nuclear pore complex had the most obvious and pervasive effects on the localization of other Nups.
source: Depletion of the Nups known to participate in the early stages of NPC formation (e.g. ELYS and NUP153), or those known to form the structural scaffold of the nuclear pore complex (e.g. NUP107 and NUP133), or those with the clear effects on cell viability (e.g. NUP93 and NUP205), had the most obvious and pervasive effects on the localization of other Nups.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their immunofluorescence data.

claim: The knockdown of several Nups (e.g. NUP188, NUP214, and NUP88) had no effect on the apparent localization of the other Nups, despite having clear effects on their protein levels.
source: Conversely, the knockdown of several Nups (e.g. NUP188, NUP214, and NUP88) had no effect on the apparent localization of the other Nups, despite having clear effects on their protein levels.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplements 1–14.

claim: Some Nups are destabilized in the absence of their NPC binding partners.
source: This finding suggests that some Nups are destabilized in the absence of their NPC binding partners.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their data.

claim: The knockdown of an individual Nup often changed the level of other Nups and the composition of NPCs in ways that were not easily predicted.
source: In general, the knockdown of an individual Nup often changed the level of other Nups and the composition of NPCs in ways that were not easily predicted.
evidence: This is the authors' summary of their observations.

claim: The nuclear accumulation of the SV40 NLS-GFP-LacZ was unaffected or only marginally affected by most Nup or NTR depletions.
source: Depletion of Nups and NTRs revealed that most perturbations allowed residual nuclear transport to proceed. Indeed, the nuclear accumulation of the SV40 NLS-GFP-LacZ was unaffected or only marginally affected by most Nup or NTR depletions.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplements 15 and 16.

claim: RANBP2 and KPNB1 depletion caused nearly complete nuclear exclusion of SV40 NLS-GFP-LacZ.
source: while RANBP2 and KPNB1 depletion caused nearly complete nuclear exclusion of SV40 NLS-GFP-LacZ.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplements 15 and 16.

claim: A larger number of Nup depletions cause partial or apparently complete inhibition of MX2(25)NLS-GFP-LacZ nuclear accumulation.
source: Moreover, a larger number of Nup depletions cause partial or apparently complete inhibition of MX2(25)NLS-GFP-LacZ nuclear accumulation.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplements 17 and 18.

claim: NUP214, NUP88, or NUP153 depletion caused near complete exclusion of MX2(25)NLS-GFP-LacZ from the nucleus, but did not affect nuclear accumulation of SV40 NLS-GFP-LacZ.
source: For example, NUP214, NUP88, or NUP153 depletion caused near complete exclusion of MX2(25)NLS-GFP-LacZ from the nucleus, but did not affect nuclear accumulation of SV40 NLS-GFP-LacZ (Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 5–8).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 5–8.

claim: At least some nuclear pores survive and retain transport activity following the knockdown of most individual Nups.
source: These experiments indicate that at least some nuclear pores survive and retain transport activity following the knockdown of most individual Nups.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their NLS-GFP-LacZ data.

claim: Nuclear transport driven by two different NLS sequences exhibited marked differences in sensitivity to perturbation by siRNA-mediated alterations of Nup or NTR levels.
source: Moreover, nuclear transport driven by two different NLS sequences exhibited marked differences in sensitivity to perturbation by siRNA-mediated alterations of Nup or NTR levels.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their NLS-GFP-LacZ data.

claim: Several Nup knockdowns (SEH1, NUP85, NUP160, SEC13, NUP98, NUP107, NUP133, NUP43, ELYS, NUP93, NUP205, NUP155, RANBP2, and NUP153), and one NTR knockdown (TNPO1) resulted in a dramatic mislocalization of MX2.
source: Several Nup knockdowns (SEH1, NUP85, NUP160, SEC13, NUP98, NUP107, NUP133, NUP43, ELYS, NUP93, NUP205, NUP155, RANBP2, and NUP153), and one NTR knockdown (TNPO1) resulted in a dramatic mislocalization of MX2 (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplements 1–10).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplements 1–10.

claim: There were no evident differences between HeLa and HT1080 cells in the Nup requirements for MX2 localization to nuclear pores.
source: There were no evident differences between HeLa and HT1080 cells in the Nup requirements for MX2 localization to nuclear pores.
evidence: This is the authors' observation from their immunofluorescence data.

claim: CPSF6 remained localized within the nucleus following all Nup/NTR depletions, with the exception of TNPO3.
source: Consistent with the finding that Nup knockdowns did not induce a generalized global block to nuclear transport (see above), CPSF6 remained localized within the nucleus following all Nup/NTR depletions, with the exception of TNPO3 [TNPO3 is known to be required for nuclear localization of CPSF6 (Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 11–14) (De Iaco et al., 2013; Fricke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 11–14 and citations.

claim: MX2 exhibited similar Nup requirements for recruitment to the NPC as did RANBP2 and NUP62.
source: Interestingly, MX2 exhibited similar Nup requirements for recruitment to the NPC as did RANBP2 and NUP62 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: MX2 required RANBP2 (but not NUP62) for NPC recruitment.
source: Additionally, MX2 required RANBP2 (but not NUP62) for NPC recruitment.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: In mitotic cells lacking a discernable nuclear envelope, the MX2-RFP fusion appeared as aggregates dispersed throughout the cell.
source: In mitotic cells lacking a discernable nuclear envelope, the MX2-RFP fusion appeared as aggregates dispersed throughout the cell (Figure 6—figure supplements 19 and 20).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplements 19 and 20.

claim: MX2 remained dispersed in the cytosol when NUP153, NUP133, and NUP98 had been recruited to the nuclear envelope during anaphase.
source: In particular, MX2 remained dispersed in the cytosol when NUP153, NUP133, and NUP98 had been recruited to the nuclear envelope, which occurs during anaphase (reviewed in (Burke and Ellenberg, 2002; Schellhaus et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplements 19 and 20 and citations.

claim: MX2 was only visualized at the nuclear envelope subsequent to the recruitment of RANBP2.
source: RANBP2 recruitment to the NPC is a late event and follows the establishment of the structural pore and the central channel (reviewed in (Burke and Ellenberg, 2002; Schellhaus et al., 2016) and MX2 was only visualized at the nuclear envelope subsequent to the recruitment of RANBP2.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplements 19 and 20 and citations.

claim: MX2 recruitment is specifically dependent of the presence of a Nup (possibly RANBP2) that is incorporated late in the assembly of the NPC.
source: These findings suggest that MX2 recruitment is specifically dependent of the presence of a Nup (possibly RANBP2) that is incorporated late in the assembly of the NPC.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their data.

claim: MX2 might interact with the NPC only as an assembled structure, rather than with a single Nup component.
source: Alternatively, MX2 might interact with the NPC only as an assembled structure, rather than with a single Nup component.
evidence: This is the authors' speculation.

claim: The MX2-RFP fusion was most strongly co-localized with NUP98, NUP133, NUP62, RANBP2, NUP88, NUP214, NUP153, and NUP50, but showed significantly less co-localization with NUP85, ELYS, and NUP35.
source: In particular, the MX2-RFP fusion was most strongly co-localized with NUP98, NUP133, NUP62, RANBP2, NUP88, NUP214, NUP153, and NUP50, but showed significantly less co-localization with NUP85, ELYS, and NUP35.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplements 1–3.

claim: NUP98, NUP133, NUP153, NUP214, RANBP2, and NUP62 colocalized well with each other and less well with ELYS, NUP35, and NUP85.
source: These differences were also reflected in the co-localization of Nups with one another (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplements 1–3). For example, NUP98, NUP133, NUP153, NUP214, RANBP2, and NUP62 colocalized well with each other and less well with ELYS, NUP35, and NUP85.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplements 1–3.

claim: These findings could be explained by varied composition of individual nuclear pores, and/or new pores assembling during interphase, in which some, but not all Nups are present within a nascent NPC.
source: These findings could be explained by varied composition of individual nuclear pores, and/or new pores assembling during interphase, in which some, but not all Nups are present within a nascent NPC.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation and speculation.

claim: It is conceivable that nuclear pores at various stages of formation could be observed within a single cell, and possible that pores formed during interphase could be compositionally or conformationally distinct from those formed post-mitosis.
source: It is therefore conceivable that nuclear pores at various stages of formation could be observed within a single cell, and possible that pores formed during interphase could be compositionally or conformationally distinct from those formed post-mitosis.
evidence: This is the authors' speculation.

claim: The apparent heterogeneity in NPC observed in immunofluorescence may reflect the occlusion of Nup antibody epitopes in a subset of NPCs.
source: It is also possible that the apparent heterogeneity in NPC observed in immunofluorescence reflects the occlusion of Nup antibody epitopes in a subset of NPCs.
evidence: This is the authors' speculation about a technical limitation.

claim: NPC heterogeneity, in some form, affects the recruitment of MX2.
source: In either case, these results suggest that NPC heterogeneity, in some form, affects the recruitment of MX2.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their data.

claim: Depletion of a number of Nups affected HIV-1WT infectivity, particularly in dividing HeLa cells.
source: Depletion of a number of Nups affected HIV-1WT infectivity, particularly in dividing HeLa cells (Figure 8A top).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8A.

claim: With the notable exceptions of RANBP2 and NUP153, Nup depletions generally had a smaller effect on HIV-1WT infection in non-dividing as compared to dividing HeLa cells.
source: Indeed, with the notable exceptions of RANBP2 and NUP153, Nup depletions generally had a smaller effect on HIV-1WT infection in non-dividing as compared to dividing HeLa cells (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8A.

claim: The effect of Nup depletion on HIV-1 infection did not always correlate with CA binding.
source: The effect of Nup depletion on HIV-1 infection did not always correlate with CA binding; for example, NUP62 knock-down had little effect on HIV-1 infectivity, despite a strong interaction with the CA tubes, while Nup107 bound only weakly to CA tubes (Figure 3), although its depletion did inhibit HIV-1 infection (Figure 8), presumably through effects on other Nups or perturbation of the overall structure of the NPC.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their data.

claim: RANBP2 knockdown inhibited HIV-1WT infection of HeLa cells.
source: In agreement with previous reports, we found that RANBP2 knockdown inhibited HIV-1WT infection of HeLa cells.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8 and is consistent with previous reports.

claim: Effects of RANBP2 knockdown on HIV-1WT were more modest (3-fold) in HT1080 and HOS cells.
source: In HT1080 and HOS cells however, effects of RANBP2 knockdown on HIV-1WT were more modest (3-fold) (Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: A number of Nup depletions caused reduction in the anti-viral activity of MX2.
source: A number of Nup depletions caused reduction in the anti-viral activity of MX2.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8.

claim: Some Nup depletions affected both the infectivity of HIV-1, and the antiviral activity of MX2 while other depletions did not reduce HIV-1 infectivity but did reduce MX2 activity.
source: Some depletions affected both the infectivity of HIV-1, and the antiviral activity of MX2 while other depletions did not reduce HIV-1 infectivity but did reduce MX2 activity.
evidence: This is the authors' summary of their observations from Figure 8.

claim: There was not a clear correlation between whether a knockdown caused apparent perturbation of the subcellular localization of MX2 and whether it caused loss of antiviral activity.
source: Curiously, there was not a clear correlation between whether a knockdown caused apparent perturbation of the subcellular localization of MX2 and whether it caused loss of antiviral activity (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is the authors' observation from Figure 8A.

claim: The effects of Nup depletion on the antiviral activity of MX2 were more pronounced in non-dividing compared to dividing HeLa cells.
source: In HeLa cells, the effects of Nup depletion on the antiviral activity of MX2 were more pronounced in non-dividing compared to dividing cells (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8A.

claim: Some Nup depletions that reduced both HIV-1 infection and MX2 activity in dividing HeLa cells, affected MX2 activity but not HIV-1 infection in non-dividing HeLa cells.
source: Moreover, some Nup depletions (SEH1, NUP85, NUP160, SEC13, NUP98, NUP107, ELYS/ACHTF1, NUP93, NUP205, NUP88, and NUP214) that reduced both HIV-1 infection and MX2 activity in dividing HeLa cells, affected MX2 activity but not HIV-1 infection in non-dividing HeLa cells.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8A.

claim: There were a number of differences in the Nup requirements for MX2 activity in HeLa and HT1080 cells.
source: A number of differences were evident in the Nup requirements for MX2 activity in HeLa and HT1080 cells.
evidence: This is the authors' summary of their observations from Figure 8.

claim: Some Nup depletions that reduced the antiviral activity of MX2 in HeLa cells, did not affect its activity in HT1080 cells.
source: Specifically, some Nup depletions that reduced the antiviral activity of MX2 in HeLa cells, did not affect its activity in HT1080 cells.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8.

claim: Several Nup/NTR depletions (e.g. NUP155, NUP54, NUPL1, RANBP2, NUP153, and KPNB1) resulted in a dramatic increase in MX2 antiviral activity, specifically in non-dividing HT1080 cells.
source: Moreover, several Nup/NTR depletions (e.g. NUP155, NUP54, NUPL1, RANBP2, NUP153, and KPNB1) resulted in a dramatic increase in MX2 antiviral activity, specifically in non-dividing HT1080 cells, while having no effect or diminishing activity in HeLa cells.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8.

claim: Both HIV-1 infection and MX2 activity were affected by Nup perturbation, and these effects were clearly cell-type and cell-cycle dependent.
source: Overall, both HIV-1 infection and MX2 activity were affected by Nup perturbation, and these effects were clearly cell-type and cell-cycle dependent.
evidence: This is the authors' summary of their observations.

claim: The N-terminal 91 amino acids of MX2 contain both the specificity determinants and the NLS.
source: The N-terminal 91 amino acids of MX2, that contain both the specificity determinants and the NLS
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The N-terminal 91 amino acids of MX2 have been shown to confer anti-HIV-1 activity when transferred to proteins that form multimers (MX1 and FV1).
source: The N-terminal 91 amino acids of MX2, that contain both the specificity determinants and the NLS, have been shown to confer anti-HIV-1 activity when transferred to proteins that form multimers (MX1 and FV1), but do not normally possess anti-HIV-1 activity (Goujon et al., 2015, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: MX2(N91)-ARFAPTIN2 was not localized at the NPC, but rather appeared to localize at the trans Golgi network, similar to authentic ARFAPTIN2.
source: Unlike MX2 and an MX2-MX1 chimera (Goujon et al., 2014), the MX2(N91)-ARFAPTIN 2 was not localized at the NPC, but rather appeared to localize at the trans Golgi network, similar to authentic ARFAPTIN2 (Peter et al., 2004) (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8—figure supplement 2A and citations.

claim: HIV-1WT was inhibited by MX2(N91)-ARFAPTIN2 and by a positive control CypA-ARFAPTIN2 fusion protein, but not ARFAPTIN2 alone or a fusion containing the N-terminal domain of MX1 (MX1(N43)-ARFAPTIN2).
source: HIV-1WT was inhibited by MX2(N91)-ARFAPTIN2 and by a positive control CypA-ARFAPTIN2 fusion protein, but not ARFAPTIN2 alone or a fusion containing the N-terminal domain of MX1 (MX1(N43)-ARFAPTIN2) (Figure 8—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8—figure supplement 2B–D.

claim: Other lentiviruses and HIV-1 CA mutants were partially or completely resistant to restriction by the MX2(N91)-ARFAPTIN2 fusion in a manner largely reflecting their relative sensitivity to full-length MX2.
source: Other lentiviruses and HIV-1 CA mutants were partially or completely resistant to restriction by the MX2(N91)-ARFAPTIN2 fusion in a manner largely reflecting their relative sensitivity to full-length MX2 (Figure 8—figure supplements 2D and 3A).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8—figure supplements 2D and 3A.

claim: Unlike full-length MX2, the MX2(N91)-ARFAPTIN2 fusion did not increase infectivity of HIV-1G89V, instead it marginally reduced HIV-1G89V infection.
source: However, unlike full-length MX2, the MX2(N91)-ARFAPTIN2 fusion did not increase infectivity of HIV-1G89V, instead it marginally reduced HIV-1G89V infection
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Like authentic MX2, the MX2(N91)-ARFAPTIN2 fusion was able to rescue the HIV-1N57S CA mutant from inhibition by CsA in HT1080 cells.
source: Conversely, like authentic MX2, the MX2(N91)-ARFAPTIN2 fusion was able to rescue the HIV-1N57S CA mutant from inhibition by CsA in HT1080 cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: The antiviral activity of the MX2(N91)-Arfaptin2 fusion was not enhanced by growth arrest in HeLa cells.
source: Moreover, the antiviral activity of the MX2(N91)-Arfaptin2 fusion was not enhanced by growth arrest in HeLa cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The requirements for Nups/NTRs in the antiviral activity of MX2(N91)- ARFAPTIN2 differed from those for MX2.
source: Notably, the requirements for Nups/NTRs in the antiviral activity of MX2(N91)- ARFAPTIN2 differed from those for MX2.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Inhibition of HIV-1 by MX2(N91)- ARFAPTIN2 was reduced by some Nup depletions, but depletion of several other Nup/NTRs that impaired MX2 activity (e.g. NUP107, NUP153, and TNPO1) did not affect MX2(N91)- ARFAPTIN2 activity.
source: Inhibition of HIV-1 by MX2(N91)- ARFAPTIN2 was reduced by some Nup depletions, but depletion of several other Nup/NTRs that impaired MX2 activity (e.g. NUP107, NUP153, and TNPO1; Figure 8A) did not affect MX2(N91)- ARFAPTIN2 activity (Figure 8—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 3C.

claim: MX2(N91)-ARFAPTIN2 occluded access of HIV-1 to nuclear DNA in an at least partly different manner to the authentic MX2 protein.
source: These observations suggest that MX2(N91)-ARFAPTIN2 occluded access of HIV-1 to nuclear DNA in an at least partly different manner to the authentic MX2 protein.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their data.

claim: HIV-2 and SIVmac infection were inhibited by many Nup depletions and both were modestly sensitive to depletions of a number of Nups that did not affect HIV-1 infection (e.g. NUP155, TPR, NUP62, NUP54, NUPL1).
source: HIV-2 and SIVmac infection were inhibited by many Nup depletions and both were modestly sensitive to depletions of a number of Nups that did not affect HIV-1 infection (e.g. NUP155, TPR, NUP62, NUP54, NUPL1 (Figure 8—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8—figure supplement 4.

claim: The MX2 sensitivity of HIV-2 and SIVmac was also differently affected by certain Nup depletions (e.g. NUP88, NUP214) as compared to HIV-1.
source: The MX2 sensitivity of HIV-2 and SIVmac was also differently affected by certain Nup depletions (e.g. NUP88, NUP214) as compared to HIV-1 (Figure 8—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8—figure supplement 4.

claim: Nup depletions generally had lesser effects on EIAV and FIV infection of HeLa cells as compared to primate lentiviruses.
source: Nup depletions generally had lesser effects on EIAV and FIV infection of HeLa cells as compared to primate lentiviruses (Figure 8—figure supplement 5A–B).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8—figure supplement 5A–B.

claim: The reduced sensitivity of EIAV and FIV to Nup depletion indicates that sensitivity of the primate lentiviruses was not merely the result of non-specific effects on cell viability or physiology, but more likely due to selective effects on nucleocytoplasmic trafficking.
source: Importantly, the reduced sensitivity of these viruses to Nup depletion indicates that sensitivity of the primate lentiviruses, HIV-1, HIV-2, and SIVmac (Figure 8, Figure 8—figure supplement 4) was not merely the result of non-specific effects on cell viability or physiology, but more likely due to selective effects on nucleocytoplasmic trafficking.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their data.

claim: Some Nup depletions that targeted members of the Nup62 subcomplex (NUP62, NUP54, NUPL1) increased FIV infection in HeLa cells.
source: Surprisingly, some Nup depletions that targeted members of the Nup62 subcomplex (NUP62, NUP54, NUPL1) increased FIV infection in HeLa cells.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8—figure supplement 5B.

claim: The majority of Nup depletions had little effect on MX2 resistance of FIV or EIAV, but some depletions marginally sensitized EIAV or FIV to inhibition by MX2 in HeLa cells (NUP205, NUP155, NUP54, NUPL1, KPNB1).
source: The majority of Nup depletions had little effect on MX2 resistance of FIV or EIAV, but some depletions marginally sensitized EIAV or FIV to inhibition by MX2 in HeLa cells (NUP205, NUP155, NUP54, NUPL1, KPNB1) (Figure 8—figure supplement 5A–B).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8—figure supplement 5A–B.

claim: There was substantial variability in the effects of Nup depletion on infection by CA mutants, as well as differential effects on CA mutants across the three cell lines.
source: Overall, there was substantial variability in the effects of Nup depletion on infection by CA mutants, as well as differential effects on CA mutants across the three cell lines (Figure 9 and Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is the authors' summary of their observations from Figure 9 and Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: HIV-1N57S was highly dependent upon certain Nups.
source: The cell cycle-dependent CA mutant, HIV-1N57S' should access target cell chromosomal DNA selectively during cell division and is therefore not expected to require intact nuclear pores for infection. However, HIV-1N57S was highly dependent upon certain Nups (Figure 9A and Figure 9—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 9A and Figure 9—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The HIV-1N57S mutant was sensitive to depletion of NUP133, particularly in HeLa cells, while WT virus was not affected by this perturbation.
source: Indeed, the HIV-1N57S mutant was sensitive to depletion of NUP133, particularly in HeLa cells, while WT virus was not affected by this perturbation (Figures 8A and 9A).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 8A and 9A.

claim: In several cases, the CA mutants exhibited reduced sensitivity to Nup depletion compared to the WT virus, particularly in HeLa cells.
source: Conversely, in several cases, the CA mutants exhibited reduced sensitivity to Nup depletion compared to the WT virus, particularly in HeLa cells.
evidence: This is the authors' observation from their data.

claim: The HIV-1T210K, HIV-1A92E, and HIV-1N57S CA mutants that were partially or completely resistant to MX2 in dividing HeLa cells, remained largely unaffected by MX2 upon Nup/NTR depletion in dividing HeLa cells.
source: Consistent with the idea that HIV-1 CA mutants fail to exploit Nups in the same way as HIV1WT, the HIV-1T210K, HIV-1A92E, and HIV-1N57S CA mutants that were partially or completely resistant to MX2 in dividing HeLa cells, remained largely unaffected by MX2 upon Nup/NTR depletion in dividing HeLa cells (Figure 9A,B and D).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 9A,B and D.

claim: The HIV-1A92E CA mutant that exhibits HIV1WT levels of infectivity in HT1080 cells was sensitive to MX2 in HT1080 cells.
source: Conversely, the HIV-1A92E CA mutant that exhibits HIV1WT levels of infectivity in HT1080 cells was sensitive to MX2 in HT1080 cells.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 9C.

claim: The MX2 sensitivity of HIV-1A92E was reduced by some Nup/NTR depletions (e.g. NUP93, NUP88, NUP214) in HT1080 cells.
source: This MX2 sensitivity was reduced by some Nup/NTR depletions (e.g. NUP93, NUP88, NUP214) (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 9C.

claim: The modest increase of HIV-1G89V infectivity exerted by MX2 could be either amplified by some Nup depletions (e.g. NUP88, NUP214) or diminished by other Nup depletions (e.g. NUP54, NUPL1, RANBP2).
source: Finally, the modest increase of HIV-1G89V infectivity exerted by MX2 could be either amplified by some Nup depletions (e.g. NUP88, NUP214) or diminished by other Nup depletions (e.g. NUP54, NUPL1, RANBP2) (Figure 9E–F).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 9E–F.

claim: In most cases, CsA addition did not modify the effect of Nup perturbation on WT HIV-1 in HeLa cells.
source: In most cases, CsA addition did not modify the effect of Nup perturbation on WT HIV-1 in HeLa cells.
evidence: This is the authors' summary of their observations from Figure 10.

claim: CsA dramatically reduced the deleterious effects of RANBP2 and NUP153 depletion on WT HIV-1 infection of HeLa cells.
source: The exception to this general finding was that CsA dramatically reduced the deleterious effects of RANBP2 and NUP153 depletion on WT HIV-1 infection of HeLa cells (Figure 10A).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 10A.

claim: CsA rescued WT HIV-1 infection of HeLa cells when RANBP2 or NUP153 were depleted.
source: Put another way, CsA rescued WT HIV-1 infection of HeLa cells when RANBP2 or NUP153 were depleted.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their data in Figure 10A.

claim: In HT1080 cells, CsA modestly reduced HIV-1 infectivity, and several Nup/NTR depletions (e.g. NUP93, NUP205, NUP155, RANBP2, NUP153, TNPO3, TNPO1, KPNB1, CPSF6) eliminated this effect.
source: Conversely, in HT1080 cells, CsA modestly reduced HIV-1 infectivity, and several Nup/NTR depletions (e.g. NUP93, NUP205, NUP155, RANBP2, NUP153, TNPO3, TNPO1, KPNB1, CPSF6) eliminated this effect (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 10B.

claim: The ability of CsA to rescue HIV-1 from the antiviral activity of MX2 was partly dependent upon Nups.
source: The ability of CsA to rescue HIV-1 from the antiviral activity of MX2 was also partly dependent upon Nups
evidence: This is the authors' summary of their observations from Figure 10.

claim: HIV-1 was rendered marginally sensitive to MX2 in CsA-treated HeLa or HT1080 cells when some Nups/NTRs were depleted (e.g. NUP160, NUP98, NUPL1, TNPO3, KPNB1).
source: HIV-1 was rendered marginally sensitive to MX2 in CsA-treated HeLa or HT1080 cells when some Nups/NTRs were depleted (e.g. NUP160, NUP98, NUPL1, TNPO3, KPNB1) (Figure 10C–D).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 10C–D.

claim: The CsA dependence of HIV-1A92E infection in HeLa cells was exaggerated by some Nup knockdowns (e.g. NUP93, NUP205, NUP54, NUP153) while other knockdowns reduced or eliminated the enhancing effects of CsA (e.g. NUP98, NUP107, NUP155).
source: The CsA dependence of HIV-1A92E infection in HeLa cells was exaggerated by some Nup knockdowns (e.g. NUP93, NUP205, NUP54, NUP153) while other knockdowns reduced or eliminated the enhancing effects of CsA (e.g. NUP98, NUP107, NUP155) (Figure 11A).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 11A.

claim: The lack of a CsA effect on the HIV-1A92E in HT1080 cells was not modified by Nup/NTR depletion, with one exception; specifically, NUP205 depletion caused HT1080 cells to exhibit the CsA-dependent phenotype characteristic of HeLa cells.
source: Conversely, the lack of a CsA effect on the HIV-1A92E in HT1080 cells (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2) was not modified by Nup/NTR depletion, with one exception; specifically, NUP205 depletion caused HT1080 cells to exhibit the CsA-dependent phenotype characteristic of HeLa cells (Figure 11B).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 11B.

claim: Infection by HIV-1N57S was strongly inhibited by CsA in HT1080 cells and Nup depletions partly (e.g. NUP62, NUP54, NUPL1) or nearly completely (e.g. NUP155, NUP205) abolished this CsA sensitivity.
source: Infection by HIV-1N57S was strongly inhibited by CsA in HT1080 cells (Figure 1) and Nup depletions partly (e.g. NUP62, NUP54, NUPL1) or nearly completely (e.g. NUP155, NUP205) abolished this CsA sensitivity, (Figure 11C–D).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 11C–D.

claim: CsA-inhibited HIV-1N57S infection was rescued by MX2, and Nup/NTR knockdowns (e.g. NUP93, NUP205, KPNB1) inhibited this rescue activity.
source: CsA-inhibited HIV-1N57S infection was rescued by MX2 (Figure 1). Nup/NTR knockdowns (e.g. NUP93, NUP205, KPNB1) inhibited this rescue activity.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 11D.

claim: MX2 knockdown itself did not completely eliminate its ability to rescue HIV-1N57S from inhibition by CsA.
source: Surprisingly, MX2 knockdown itself did not completely eliminate its ability to rescue HIV-1N57S from inhibition by CsA.
evidence: This is the authors' observation from their data.

claim: Sub-detectable levels of MX2 are required for the rescue of HIV-1N57S from CsA inhibition.
source: This finding suggests that sub-detectable levels of MX2 are required for this effect.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their observation.

claim: The positive and negative effects of CypA and MX2 on HIV-1 infection were clearly dependent on Nups.
source: Overall, the positive and negative effects of CypA and MX2 on HIV-1 infection were clearly dependent on Nups.
evidence: This is the authors' summary of their observations.

claim: There was significant overlap in the identity of Nups and NTRs that mediate MX2 and CypA effects on HIV-1 infection.
source: Moreover, there was significant overlap in the identity of Nups and NTRs that mediate MX2 and CypA effects on HIV-1 infection.
evidence: This is the authors' summary of their observations.

claim: MX2 did not affect the nuclear import driven by canonical NLS sequences found in SV40, Nucleoplasmin, or HTLV-1 Rex, and only marginally inhibited DDX21 NLS driven import.
source: MX2 did not affect the nuclear import driven by canonical NLS sequences found in SV40, Nucleoplasmin, or HTLV-1 Rex, and only marginally inhibited DDX21 NLS driven import (Figure 12)
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 12.

claim: The accumulation of GFP-LacZ in the nucleus driven by NLS signals from C-MYC, and especially HNRNP K, as well as the NLS from MX2 itself, was clearly inhibited by MX2.
source: In contrast, the accumulation GFP-LacZ in the nucleus driven by NLS signals from C-MYC, and especially HNRNP K, as well as the NLS from MX2 itself, was clearly inhibited by MX2.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 12.

claim: MX2 does not appear to induce a global block to nuclear import but can inhibit the movement of a non-viral cargo protein from the cytoplasm to the nucleus, in a manner that is highly dependent on the nature of the NLS.
source: Thus, these data indicate that MX2 does not appear to induce a global block to nuclear import but can inhibit the movement of a non-viral cargo protein from the cytoplasm to the nucleus, in a manner that is highly dependent on the nature of the NLS, and by inference, the 'pathway' taken into the nucleus.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their data in Figure 12.
